The Cape mole-rat (Georychus capensis) is a solitary, subterranean rodent endemic to the Western and Eastern Cape provinces of South Africa. Females of this species give birth to a single litter each year, with a mean litter size of approximately 3 to 4 pups per litter [N_R_i = approximately 3 to 4 pups per litter] under controlled laboratory conditions. This annual reproductive event results in a reproductive frequency of one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year]. Newborn pups are altricial and weigh approximately 6 grams [Wwb = approximately 6 grams] at birth, a modest neonatal mass typical of many bathyergid rodents. The gestation period lasts 44 days [tg = 44 days] when the female's body temperature is maintained at 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C], reflecting the relatively short intrauterine development characteristic of this lineage.

Weaning occurs relatively early in the developmental trajectory of this mole-rat. The pups reach a wet weight of approximately 36 grams [Wwx = approximately 36 grams] at the time of nutritional independence from the dam. This weaning event typically occurs at around 28 days after birth [tx = around 28 days after birth] when measured under stable thermal conditions at 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]. The relatively rapid transition from a milk-dependent diet to solid food consumption is facilitated by the mother's provisioning of underground corms and geophytes, which are the primary dietary items for this species. After weaning, the young individuals disperse from the natal burrow system to establish their own territories. The comparatively modest body mass at weaning suggests that post-weaning growth must be substantial before these juveniles can attain the body size necessary for successful burrow excavation and independent foraging in the fynbos soils they inhabit.

Juvenile mole-rats exhibit a prolonged period of somatic growth following weaning before reaching sexual maturity. Body mass increases steadily until individuals approach their ultimate adult dimensions, with the maximum recorded adult wet weight being approximately 181 grams [Wwi = approximately 181 grams]. The attainment of puberty occurs at around 304 days after birth [tp = around 304 days after birth] under standard housing conditions at 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]. This relatively late onset of reproductive capability, nearly a full year post-partum, is consistent with the species' K-selected life-history strategy and its occupation of a stable, low-disturbance subterranean niche. The considerable gap between weaning and puberty allows for extensive foraging experience and the establishment of a robust burrow system, both of which are critical for successful reproduction.

The maximum lifespan of Georychus capensis has been documented in captive populations, with the oldest recorded individuals surviving for approximately 4088 days [am = approximately 4088 days] at a body temperature of 36.4 °C [T = 36.4 °C]. This longevity, equivalent to over 11 years, is remarkably extended for a rodent of this body size and aligns with the pattern of extended lifespans observed in other subterranean bathyergids, most notably the naked mole-rat (Heterocephalus glaber). Such extreme longevity likely reflects the low extrinsic mortality rates associated with a fossorial lifestyle, including protection from aerial predators and a relatively stable thermal microenvironment. The species' slow rate of senescence and delayed reproductive schedule are typical of mammals that inhabit predictable, resource-rich underground environments. Current comparative research continues to investigate the physiological mechanisms that underpin this extended lifespan, with particular focus on oxidative stress resistance and cellular maintenance pathways.

Reproductive output in this species is constrained by both the small litter size and the annual breeding frequency. Under optimal conditions, the maximum annual fecundity reaches approximately 12 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 12 offspring per year], a value that would be achieved by a single annual litter [F_R_i = a single annual litter], of 12 pups [N_R_i = of 12 pups]. Field observations, however, suggest that typical litter sizes are considerably smaller, averaging 3 to 5 pups, and that some females may skip breeding entirely in years of low rainfall or reduced food availability. The ecological constraints of the fynbos habitat, including seasonal fluctuations in the availability of underground storage organs, heavily influence female reproductive success and pup survival. This conservative reproductive strategy, combined with the species' remarkable longevity and delayed maturity, underscores the Cape mole-rat's adaptation to a stable but energetically challenging subterranean environment that rewards persistence over rapid turnover.
